title: Splinting a suspected broken arm or leg
asks: how do I splint a broken arm
how to splint a broken leg
I think my ankle is broken what do I do
broken bone in the woods how to immobilize it
bone sticking out of the skin what do I do
how to make a splint from sticks
possible fx lower leg how to splint
should I straighten a broken leg
answer: Signs that an arm or leg might be broken: significant pain with marked swelling, a "snap" heard or felt, a different length or shape of the limb, loss of pulse or feeling in the limb, or a crackling or popping sound under the skin.

Get medical help: a splint only supports the fracture until the person receives medical treatment. If the limb is numb, tingling, cold, or pale to bluish, get the person to medical treatment as soon as possible: prompt treatment may prevent loss of the limb.
An open fracture (a wound near the break, or bone sticking out) will require cleaning and possibly surgery: plan to get the person to a surgical unit after splinting.
If a back or neck injury is suspected, do not move the person unless there is immediate life-threatening danger, such as a fire or an explosion.
First be ready to deal with anything life-threatening. If it is an open fracture, stop the bleeding, and cover all wounds with dressings before splinting.
Splint a suspected fracture before the person is moved, if circumstances permit, unless the scene is unsafe.
Loosen tight clothing and take all jewelry off the injured part. Leave boots on unless there is bleeding from the foot or they are needed to stabilize a neck injury.
Check circulation below the injury: skin color (pale, white or bluish-gray may mean impaired circulation), temperature compared with the uninjured side, and any numbness, tightness, cold or tingling.

Get splints long enough to immobilize the joint above and the joint below the break: boards, poles, sticks, tree limbs or cardboard. If nothing is available, the chest wall can be used to immobilize a broken arm, and the uninjured leg to immobilize a broken leg.
Pad the splints where they touch any bony part, such as the elbow, wrist, knee, ankle, crotch or armpit.
If the limb has a good pulse, do not straighten it or force it back into line: splint it in the position found.

Place a splint on each side of the break and tie them in place above and below it with cravats, strips of cloth or belts: if possible at least four ties, two above and two below. Tie the knots on the splint, away from the body, and never directly over the break.
Recheck circulation after splinting. If there is numbness, tingling or increased pain, or the fingers or toes turn pale or bluish, loosen the bandage.
For an arm, add a sling: the hand higher than the elbow, the fingers always showing.
Keep checking the splinted limb: swelling may increase.
warnings: If the bone is sticking out of the skin, do not try to push it back under the skin. Put a dressing over the wound to protect the area.
Improper movement of a person with a back or neck injury may cause permanent paralysis or death.
If the limb is obviously deformed, do not make the person move it.
Do not tie a splint on with wire or cord: narrow material could damage tissue and act like a tourniquet.
Do not wrap the splint too tightly: it may cut off circulation below the splint.

quotes.text: The warning signs that an arm or leg might be fractured include: • Significant pain along with marked swelling. • An audible or perceived "snap." • Different length or shape of limb. • Loss of pulse or sensation in the injured arm or leg. • Crepitus (a crackling or popping sound under the skin).
Evaluate the casualty and be prepared to perform any necessary lifesaving measures. Monitor the casualty for development of conditions that may require you to perform necessary lifesaving measures.

Loosen any tight or binding clothing. • Remove all jewelry from the injured part and place it in the casualty's pocket. Tell the casualty you are doing this because if the jewelry is not removed and swelling occurs later, they may not be able remove it and further bodily injury could result. • Boots should not be removed from the casualty unless they are needed to stabilize a neck injury, or there is actual bleeding from the foot.

Check the circulation below the site of the injury. • Note any pale, white, or bluish-gray color of the skin, which may indicate impaired circulation. • Check the temperature of the injured extremity. Use your hand to compare the temperature of the injured side with the uninjured side. The body area below the injury may be colder to the touch indicating poor circulation. • Question the casualty about the presence of numbness, tightness, cold, or tingling sensations.

Ensure that splints are long enough to immobilize the joint above and below the suspected fracture. If possible, use at least four ties (two above and two below the fracture) to secure the splints. The ties should be square knots and should be tied away from the body on the splint. Distal pulses of the affected extremity should be checked before and after the application of the splint.

Splints may be improvised from such items such as boards, poles, sticks, tree limbs, or cardboard. If nothing is available for a splint, the chest wall can be used to immobilize a fractured arm, and the uninjured leg can be used to immobilize (to some extent) the fractured leg.

Pad the splints where they touch any bony part of the body, such as the elbow, wrist, knee, ankle, crotch, or armpit areas. Padding prevents excessive pressure on the area, which could lead to circulation problems.

Splinting the fracture in the position found. DO NOT attempt to reposition or straighten the injury. If it is an open fracture, stop the bleeding and protect the wound. • Covering all wounds with field dressings before applying a splint.
Do not force realignment of a deformed limb if the limb has a good pulse.

Consider an open fracture if there is a wound near a fracture site. Open fracture sites can often be contaminated and will require cleaning and potentially surgical debridement before the fracture can be fixed. If an open fracture is suspected, plan for handover/transfer to a surgical or orthopaedic unit after splinting.

Placing one splint on each side of the fracture. Make sure that the splints reach, if possible, beyond the joints above and below the fracture. • Tying the splints by— ▪ Securing each splint in place above and below the fracture site with cravats, or improvised material. Improvised materials, such as gauze bandage, strips of cloth, belts, or whatever other materials you have, may be used.
Tie all knots on the splint away from the casualty (figure 13-3). DO NOT tie knots directly over the suspected fracture site.

Caution must be taken when splinting to ensure that it is not wrapped too tightly. If wrapped too tightly, the splint may cut off circulation below the splint. If there is numbness, tingling or increased pain, or if the fingers or toes turn pale or bluish, loosen the bandage. Increased swelling may occur; continued monitoring of the splintered fracture is required.
RECHECK the circulation after application of the splint. Check the skin color and temperature. This is to ensure that the bandages holding the splint in place have not been tied too tightly.
Remember that the casualty's hand should be higher than their elbow, and their fingers should be always showing. The sling should be applied so that the supporting pressure is on the uninjured side.

During the TFC phase, it is highly advisable to splint all fractures if circumstances permit. Splinting is crucial to immobilize the affected area, preventing further damage, and minimizing pain for the casualty. Proper splinting techniques ensure that fractures are adequately supported until the injured individual receives comprehensive medical treatment.

The candidate will list (or select the answer that lists) the circumstances when a victim should be moved from the scene by indicating both of the following: (1) after suspected fractures have been immobilized and severe bleeding has been stopped; (2) movement is necessary due to an unsafe scene or in order to further treat the victim.
Note. With the presence of an obvious deformity, do not make the casualty move the extremity. • Look for an unnatural position of the extremity. • Look for a bone sticking out (protruding).

Casualties with fractures of the extremities may show impaired circulation, such as numbness, tingling, cold or pale to bluish skin tone. These casualties should be evacuated to medical personnel and treated as soon as possible. Prompt medical treatment may prevent possible loss of the limb.
If it is an open fracture and the bone is protruding from the skin, DO NOT ATTEMPT TO PUSH THE BONE BACK UNDER THE SKIN. Apply a field dressing over the wound to protect the area.

Unless there is immediate life-threatening danger, such as a fire or an explosion, DO NOT move the casualty with a suspected back or neck injury. Improper movement may cause permanent paralysis or death.
Narrow materials such as wire, or cord should not be used to secure a splint in place. The application of wire or narrow material to an extremity could cause tissue damage and a TQ effect.

conflict: STRAIGHTENING A DEFORMED LIMB THAT HAS NO PULSE (the card states only the case all sources agree on: good pulse = do not straighten): ATP 4-02.11 (2026) para 13-34 says splint in the position found and DO NOT attempt to reposition or straighten (its own para 13-19 says apply the splint with the limb in the position of function or a normal resting position if possible); ATP 3-50.21 (2018) says 'Only reposition the break if there is no blood flow'; WHO-ICRC Basic Emergency Care 2018 (trained providers) says if the limb is visibly deformed and pulses beyond the fracture are weak or absent, first straighten (reduce) the fracture before splinting; HHS Ship's Medicine Chest 2003 (crew first-aid assessment standard) expects 'proper traction' when immobilizing a simple limb fracture. FEMA P-2064 (2020) has no fracture first aid.
